clue.text: Cider from the wood-but not from this

definitions.text: Cider from the wood-but not from this

parts.words: Cider from the wood-but not from this
parts.note: cider drawn from the cask comes from apples, but the gall that grows on an oak tree only looks like fruit and makes no drink

explanation.surface: A drinker praises cask cider while ruling out one source of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the wood' means drawn from the barrel, but it tempts you to think of a tree; the oak's ball-shaped gall is called an apple yet yields no cider.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a round gall formed on oak twigs by a wasp larva, an apple in shape only.

clue.text: Posture of a striker, perhaps ?

parts.note: one who 'strikes' a pose adopts a stance, so the striker here is a poser, not a footballer or a worker on strike

explanation.surface: A coach studies how a batsman or footballer stands.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'to strike an attitude', meaning to take up a theatrical pose; the striker is the person doing that.
explanation.definitionFit: A posture or bodily stance is one sense of the word, as in the idiom about adopting a dramatic pose.

clue.text: It's a secondary consideration.

parts.note: secondary read as 'coming second in time': a thought that occurs later than the first one

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a matter as of minor importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secondary' looks like 'less important', but here it means coming second, a later idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Such an idea is one added later, a consideration that comes second in time.

clue.text: "I have taken all knowledge to be my ——" (Bacon)

definitions.text: "I have taken all knowledge to be my ——" (Bacon)

parts.words: "I have taken all knowledge to be my ——" (Bacon)
parts.note: a famous line from Francis Bacon's letter to Lord Burghley, with the final word left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A quotation from the philosopher Francis Bacon with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill-in-the-blank quotation: Bacon wrote in 1592 that he had taken all knowledge to be his domain or sphere.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means a sphere or field of activity, a region of authority claimed as one's own.

clue.text: A girl has no real following in Worcestershire

indicators.note: the phrase meaning not genuine comes after the girl's name, so it is placed second in the build

parts.note: Eve is a girl's name
a sham is a fake, something not real

explanation.surface: A young woman finds she has no genuine supporters in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a noun (her fans), but it only says the second piece comes after the first. EVESHAM is a market town in Worcestershire, a county in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a market town located in that Midlands county, so the definition places it geographically.

clue.text: Resting-place for flood survivors

parts.note: in Genesis, Noah's ark came to rest on a mountain after the waters of the great flood went down

explanation.surface: A shelter is needed for people rescued from a modern flood.
explanation.walkthrough: The flood is Noah's, and the survivors are those in the ark, which grounded on this Turkish mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis says the ark settled on the mountains of this name in eastern Turkey once the deluge subsided.

clue.text: Soldiers get no synchronization out of it

definitions.text: Soldiers get no synchronization out of it

parts.words: Soldiers get no synchronization out of it
parts.note: soldiers who are 'out of' this marching unit are not keeping in time with each other

explanation.surface: A drill sergeant complains that the troops cannot keep together.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'out of step' means not marching in time; soldiers out of it are not synchronised.
explanation.definitionFit: In marching, the regular pace taken together is this word, and being outside it means losing time.

clue.text: A prude's self-description is at the beginning

parts.note: a prude would describe herself as 'I'm prim', run together as IMPRIM

explanation.surface: Someone notes that prim self-portraits come first.
explanation.walkthrough: The prude says 'I'm prim'; add IS. IMPRIMIS is Latin for 'in the first place', used when listing items.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adverb means firstly or in the first place, so it opens a list.

clue.text: Word for word-an uncommonly brave boy

indicators.note: done in an uncommon way, so the letters of the word brave are put in an unusual order

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A bold lad is praised, word for word as reported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncommonly' turns BRAVE into VERBA, and TIM follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived adverb means exactly as spoken or written, repeating each term unchanged.

clue.text: Steer the children back

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word for small children from end to start

parts.note: tots are small children

explanation.surface: Someone guides the youngsters home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a young castrated bullock, called a STOT in Scotland and northern England. 'Back' turns TOTS around.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect word for a young bullock or ox, so the young castrated male animal.

clue.text: He listens-in without a licence

parts.note: listening-in was the old term for radio listening, which needed a licence; this listener is unlicensed because he overhears others

explanation.surface: A radio fan tunes in without paying for the required licence.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1950s British radio listeners needed a licence; this one 'listens in' on private talk instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who secretly overhears others' private conversations, so a listener with no permission.

clue.text: I hear prisons might hold churchgoers

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase might hold another arrangement, so they are to be reordered

explanation.surface: Someone has heard that jails might keep worshippers locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might hold' looks like a container, but it signals an anagram of I HEAR PRISONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a local church congregation attend services there, so they are churchgoers.

clue.text: He narrowly misses being a 17

parts.note: clue 17 is an outsider; someone who only just avoids that fate is barely inside the group

explanation.surface: A man almost ends up as the thing described at 17 down.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 down is OUTSIDER; read the answer as two words, 'just in', to see why he is narrowly not one. Justin is also a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Split, the man's name gives 'barely inside', the opposite of being left out.

clue.text: A bit of a mess, needing more NATO manoeuvre

indicators.note: a manoeuvre moves things about, so the letters of more NATO are reshuffled into a new order

explanation.surface: A military shambles calls for further alliance exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'mess' is an officers' mess, the military dining building, not a muddle; an ANTEROOM is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In an officers' mess the lounge beside the dining room is so called, so it is one part of the building.

clue.text: He's keen to make his mark in the river

indicators.note: in says the word for casting a ballot sits inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
voters mark a cross on the ballot paper

explanation.surface: An ambitious swimmer hopes to distinguish himself in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make his mark' suggests achievement, but it means mark a ballot paper: VOTE goes in DEE.
explanation.definitionFit: An enthusiast or fervent follower is eager about his cause, so he is keen.

clue.text: Politician expresses vexation about a come-back

indicators.note: about means the exclamation goes round the turned word

parts.note: 'Drat!' is an exclamation of annoyance

indicators.note: back, the end of come-back, says to turn the word come around

parts.note: the first part of the hyphenated word, taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician shows annoyance when a rival stages a return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come-back' looks like one noun, but 'back' turns COME into EMOC, which DRAT surrounds ('about').
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a political party, especially the US one of that name, is a politician.

clue.text: Costers might find the change bracing

definitions.note: here a noun: things that brace or support, like the plural answer

indicators.note: change says to alter the order of the letters of costers

explanation.surface: Street sellers find a fresh breeze invigorating.
explanation.walkthrough: Costers are costermongers, London street sellers of fruit. 'Bracing' looks like 'invigorating', but it means support garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff undergarments give support to the body, so they provide bracing.

clue.text: He doesn't get a look-in; but who else could ?

definitions.text: He doesn't get a look-in; but who else could ?

parts.words: He doesn't get a look-in; but who else could ?
parts.note: a person with no chance is excluded, yet only someone standing beyond a window or door can look in

explanation.surface: Someone is left out, though others claim nobody could have had better chance.
explanation.walkthrough: A rank 'outsider' has no chance, no look-in; literally, only someone outside can look in.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-shot competitor with little chance stands, literally, beyond the inner circle.

clue.text: It compelled people to pay their way

definitions.text: It compelled people to pay their way

parts.words: It compelled people to pay their way
parts.note: 'pay their way' read literally: travellers had to hand over money to pass along a road

explanation.surface: Something forced people to be financially independent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay their way' usually means cover one's own costs; here it means paying to use the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrier on a turnpike road where a fee was charged before travellers could pass.

clue.text: Difficulties for the navigator

definitions.meaning: hardship or distress, as in being in dire financial trouble
narrow sea passages that a navigator must find a course through

explanation.surface: A sailor runs into trouble at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural means hardship, as in 'dire straits', and also narrow sea channels between landmasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Troubled circumstances are one sense; narrow waterways a sailor steers through are the other.

clue.text: Basingstoke abated her Gilbertian madness

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore, the mad heroine is calmed whenever she hears the word Basingstoke

explanation.surface: A Hampshire town soothed a woman's operatic lunacy.
explanation.walkthrough: Mad Margaret in Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore is brought to her senses by the word 'Basingstoke', a Hampshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: The deranged heroine of that comic opera bears this name and is known as Mad Margaret.

clue.text: Just the thing for junketing

parts.note: junketing suggests partying, but junket is also a milk dessert set by an enzyme from a calf's stomach

explanation.surface: Something is ideal for a lavish trip or party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junketing' looks like feasting or freebie travel, but junket is a sweet curdled-milk pudding, set with RENNET.
explanation.definitionFit: Curdled-milk desserts are set by this enzyme preparation, so it makes junket.

clue.text: Not much to eat

definitions.meaning: a small or insignificant amount, as in 'a mere bagatelle'
a layered pudding of sponge cake, fruit, custard and cream

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a meagre snack.
explanation.walkthrough: A small amount is one sense; the other is the British pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny, insignificant amount is one sense; a layered dessert of sponge and custard is the other.

clue.text: One example of those goings-on

parts.note: goings-on read literally as acts of carrying on further rather than as scandalous behaviour

explanation.surface: Someone gives an instance of suspicious behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goings-on' suggests misconduct, but here it means going on, carrying further.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrying on further is the act of going on, so one instance is a sequel or extension.

clue.text: Green missing? Then it's all off

definitions.text: Green missing? Then it's all off

parts.words: Green missing? Then it's all off
parts.note: a green light means 'go', so without it there is ... and the plan is cancelled

explanation.surface: A golfer finds the putting area gone and calls off the game.
explanation.walkthrough: Green is the 'go' light, not a golf green; without go the arrangement is off.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means impossible or cancelled, a situation where nothing proceeds.

clue.text: He was done out of his rights by a smooth character

definitions.text: He was done out of his rights by a smooth character

parts.words: He was done out of his rights by a smooth character
parts.note: in Genesis, Jacob, described as a smooth man, tricked his hairy twin out of his birthright and blessing

explanation.surface: A man was swindled out of his entitlements by a slick operator.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'smooth character' is Jacob, called 'a smooth man' in Genesis 27, as against his hairy brother.
explanation.definitionFit: The hairy elder twin in Genesis sold his birthright for pottage and lost his father's blessing to Jacob.

clue.text: "Rightly to be great Is not to stir without great ——" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Rightly to be great Is not to stir without great ——" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "Rightly to be great Is not to stir without great ——" (Hamlet)
parts.note: a line from Hamlet's soliloquy in Act 4 Scene 4, with the closing word left blank for the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill-in-the-blank quotation: Hamlet says true greatness does not act without great cause or reason.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word here means a cause or matter of dispute, a reason worth acting on.

clue.text: Underlines the direction to the locks

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south, a compass direction
tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: Someone emphasises the instructions for getting to the canal locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests canal locks or door locks, but it means hair: S goes before TRESSES ('to' is a link).
explanation.definitionFit: To emphasise is to give weight to, as underlining a word does on the page.
